title: older than ... more expensive than ...
subtitle: than me / than I am
summary: Use than after a comparative to compare two people or two things.

lesson.heading: than after a comparative
lesson.text: A woman and a man are standing together. The woman says 'I'm taller than you.' So she's **taller than** him. A hotel list shows the Europa at 140 pounds a night and the Grand at 130 pounds. The Europa Hotel is **more expensive than** the Grand. We use **than** after a comparative.

examples.text: It's **easier** to take a taxi **than** to take the bus.
'How are you today?' 'Not bad. **Better than** yesterday.'
The restaurant is **more crowded than** usual.

lesson.heading: than me / than I am
rows: I can run faster than **he can**.
You are a better singer than **me**.
You are a better singer than **I am**.
I got up earlier than **she did**.
lesson.note: After **than** we use *me / him / her / us / them*, not *I / he / she*.

lesson.heading: more than / less than
lesson.text: We also use **than** after **more** and **less**. **more than 50** means 51, 60, 80 ... **less than 50** means 49, 40, 20 ...

examples.text: *A:* How much did your shoes cost? Fifty pounds? *B:* No, **more than** that.
The film was very short - **less than** an hour.
They've got **more money than** they need.

lesson.heading: a bit older / much older
lesson.text: Box A is only a little bigger than Box B, so Box A is **a bit bigger** than Box B. Box C is very much bigger than the small Box D, so Box C is **much bigger** than Box D.

examples.text: Sue is **a bit older than** Gary - she's 25 and he's 24.
The hotel was **much more expensive than** I expected.
You go out **much more than** me.

lesson.text: After a comparative we use **than**, not *as*: *Athens is older than Rome*, not ~~older as Rome~~.

exercises.prompt: Liz is 26 and Ben is 24. Liz is ___ Ben.
Liz is 1 metre 68 tall. Ben is 1 metre 63. Liz is ___ Ben.
exercises.explanation: tall is a short word: taller than.

exercises.prompt: Liz starts work at 8 o'clock. Ben starts work at 8.30. Liz starts work ___ Ben.
exercises.explanation: early ends in -y, so the comparative is earlier.

exercises.prompt: Liz doesn't work very hard. Ben works very hard. Ben works ___ Liz.
exercises.explanation: hard is an adverb here: harder than.

exercises.prompt: Ben is very patient. Liz isn't very patient. Which sentence is right?
options: Ben is more patient than Liz.
Ben is more patient as Liz.
exercises.explanation: patient is a long word (more patient) and we use than after the comparative.

exercises.prompt: Match each sentence with the sentence about you.

pairs.left: I'm not a very good cook.
pairs.right: You're a better cook than me.
You can run faster than me.

pairs.left: They didn't get up very early.
pairs.right: You got up earlier than them.

exercises.prompt: Ben has got a lot of money. Liz hasn't got much money. Ben has got ___ Liz.
exercises.explanation: more + noun + than: more money than.

exercises.prompt: The film was very short - ___ an hour.
exercises.explanation: We say less than for a smaller number or amount.

exercises.prompt: Emma is 25. Gary is 24 and a half. Emma is ___ than Gary.
exercises.explanation: The difference is small, so we say a bit older.

exercises.prompt: Jack's mother is 52. His father is 69. Jack's mother is ___ than his father.
exercises.explanation: The difference is big, so we say much younger.

exercises.statement: Canada is much bigger as France.
exercises.explanation: Canada is much bigger than France. After a comparative we use than, not as.

exercises.prompt: You paid a lot of money for the hotel. Put the sentence in order.
exercises.answer: The hotel was much more expensive than I expected.
